mk-deal-1.title: M&A
mk-deal-1.merke: Samme form som Mannesmann-eksemplet i forelesning 16 (54:58 til 1:22:12)
mk-deal-1.body:
In September rumours spread that the French drug maker Marveaux Pharma SA (A) would bid for the German biotech firm Lindgau Biotech AG (T). Today A has made a formal offer: if the deal goes through, each T share will be exchanged for 36 new A shares. The deal will be completed or fail in exactly three months. A has 7,200 million shares outstanding and T has 150 million.

Before the rumours the share prices were PA,0 = €2.75 and PT,0 = €84.00. Today they are PA,1 = €2.95 and PT,1 = €101.20. The risk-free rate is 4% a year, compounded annually. Short selling is allowed. If the deal fails, assume that both prices return to their levels before the rumours. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is A's offer worth per T share at today's prices? What premium over T's price before the rumours is that, in percent? What fraction of the combined company would T's shareholders own?
parts.solution:
Offer value. One T share becomes 36 A shares: 36 × €2.95 = €106.20 per T share at today's prices.

Premium. 106.20/84.00 − 1 = 26.43% over T's price before the rumours. T trades at €101.20, €5.00 below the offer: the market is not sure that the deal will go through.

Ownership. A issues 36 × 150 million = 5,400 million new shares. T's shareholders would own 5,400/(7,200 + 5,400) = 5,400/12,600 = 42.86% of the combined company and A's old shareholders 57.14%. The large exchange ratio only reflects that an A share is cheap: A has many more shares than T.
criteria: Offer value 36 × 2.95 = €106.20 per T share at today's A price; 36 × 2.75 = 99.00 is the offer at the old prices.
Premium 106.20/84.00 − 1 = 26.43% over the price before the rumours.
Fraction for T's shareholders: 5,400 million new shares out of 12,600 million, so 42.86%. Dividing by A's old 7,200 million shares only gives 75%, which is wrong.
Part a is the easy part: 1 point for each number.

parts.label: b
parts.body: By how much did the market values of A and T change from before the rumours to today? What do the changes suggest about the deal's total gains and who captures them?
parts.solution:
Changes in market value (€ million).

FirmCalculationChange
A7,200 × (2.95 − 2.75)+1,440
T150 × (101.20 − 84.00)+2,580
Together+4,020

Reading. Both values rose although the deal may still fail, so the market expects the combination to add value in total. T's shareholders capture the larger part through the premium A offers, but A's shareholders gain too: the market does not think A is overpaying.

Caveat. The changes are weighted by the chance that the deal goes through. Part of them may also come from other news during the rumour period: firms do not exist in a vacuum, as the lecture warns about prices taken too early (recording 16, 54:33).
criteria: Change for A: 7,200 million × 0.20 = €1,440 million; for T: 150 million × 17.20 = €2,580 million (1 point each).
Reading (1 point): the combined value rose by €4,020 million, so the market expects total gains; T's shareholders get most of them, but A's shareholders gain too, so A is not seen as overpaying.
Bonus, not required: the changes are weighted by the chance of completion and may include other news from the rumour period.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Today you buy one T share, short-sell the 36 A shares it would be exchanged for and invest the short-sale proceeds at the risk-free rate. What is the position worth in three months if the deal goes through? If it fails?
parts.solution:
Step 1. The position today.

LegActionCash flow today (€)
Long targetBuy 1 T share at 101.20−101.20
Short acquirerShort-sell 36 A shares at 2.95+106.20
Risk-freeInvest the 106.20 for three months−106.20
Net outlay−101.20

Step 2. Three months of interest. T = 3/12 = 0.25 years, so the factor is 1.040.25 = 1.009853. The deposit grows to 106.20 × 1.009853 = 107.2464.

Step 3. The deal goes through. The T share is converted into 36 A shares, which you hand back to close the short. Only the deposit is left: €107.2464.

Step 4. The deal fails. Both prices return to their levels before the rumours. You sell the T share at 84.00 and buy back 36 A shares at 2.75, which costs 99.00: 107.2464 + 84.00 − 99.00 = €92.2464.

Check. The two payoffs differ by 99.00 − 84.00 = 15.00, what you lose on the shares if the deal fails. The position cost you €101.20 out of your own pocket.
criteria: Long 1 T and short 36 A (the exchange ratio), with the 106.20 from the short sale invested at the risk-free rate; the cost out of pocket is 101.20.
Success: 106.20 × 1.009853 = €107.2464, since the converted T share closes the short.
Failure: 107.2464 + 84.00 − 36 × 2.75 = €92.2464, at the prices before the rumours.
Other consistent constructions are accepted, for example several T shares with the matching number of A shares.

parts.label: d
parts.body: What probability of completion do today's prices imply? (If you could not solve (c), use €108.00 for success and €93.00 for failure.)
parts.solution:
Step 1. The certainty equivalent of the cost. The position cost 101.20 today. If the market prices it fairly, its expected payoff in three months equals that cost grown at the risk-free rate: 101.20 × 1.009853 = 102.1972. Do not plug in 101.20 itself.

Step 2. Solve. 102.1972 = p × 107.2464 + (1 − p) × 92.2464
p = (102.1972 − 92.2464)/(107.2464 − 92.2464) = 9.9507/15.0000 = 0.6634 (66.34%)

The same equation in present values: 101.20 = [p × 107.2464 + (1 − p) × 92.2464]/1.040.25.

Check. 0.663382 × 107.2464 + 0.336618 × 92.2464 = 102.1972 ✓. T at 101.20 lies between its failure price 84.00 and the offer value 106.20.

With the values given in the question. p = (102.1972 − 93.00)/(108.00 − 93.00) = 0.6131 (61.31%), full marks if the method is right.

The traps. Using 101.20 instead of the certainty equivalent gives 0.5969. Ignoring the interest altogether gives 0.6667. A full year (1.04) in both (c) and (d) gives 0.6533: wrong, but it is the same error as in (c) and is penalised only there. Simple interest, 1 + 0.04 × 0.25, gives 0.6633: close enough, but the course uses (1 + rf)T.
criteria: Certainty equivalent 101.20 × 1.04^0.25 = 102.1972. Plugging in 101.20 gives 0.5969 and loses most of the points.
Follow-through: with the values given in the question, p = 0.6131. A student who used 1.04 instead of 1.04^0.25 in (c) and here gets 0.6533 and loses the points for the factor only once, in (c).
Reasonable rounding is fine; show the equation.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Is the position in (c) an arbitrage? Would you advise a private investor to put most of her savings into it? How can a professional merger-arbitrage fund make such trades pay? (3–4 sentences)
parts.solution:
Model answer. No, it is not an arbitrage: compared with the risk-free alternative (102.1972), you gain 5.05 if the deal goes through but lose 9.95 if it fails. At the market's probability the expected payoff is exactly the cost grown at the risk-free rate. For a private investor with one deal this is an all-or-nothing bet: a failure costs 8.85% in three months (from 101.20 to 92.25), so most of her savings would ride on one event. A fund earns more than the risk-free rate only if the true chance of completion is higher than the implied one, that is if the spread carries a premium for bearing deal risk, or if it picks deals better than the market; spreading its capital over many largely independent deals then makes that excess return reliable instead of a gamble.

Also accepted. The calculation rests on the strong assumption that prices return to their levels before the rumours; if they would not, the true risk differs from the model's. The lecture makes the same point: a small investor «would lose quite a bit of money» if the deal fails, while big funds spread their bets over many deals (recording 16, 1:22:46). Evidence on merger arbitrage (Mitchell and Pulvino, 2001) shows losses concentrated in sharp market declines, when many deals fail together, so the risk is not fully diversifiable.
criteria: Not an arbitrage (1 point): the position loses if the deal fails (92.2464 against a certainty equivalent of 102.1972); at the market's p its expected payoff equals the cost grown at the risk-free rate.
Private investor (1 point): one deal is a concentrated all-or-nothing bet; a failure costs about 8.8% in three months.

Fund (1 point): it beats the risk-free rate only if the true probability is above the implied one (the spread carries a risk premium) or if it picks deals well. Diversification alone does not create a return: a diversified set of fairly priced bets still earns only the risk-free rate.

Fourth point: diversification over many independent deals makes the fund's return reliable, or naming the strong assumption that prices return to their levels before the rumours. Bonus: failures cluster in market crashes, so the risk is not fully diversifiable.

mk-deal-2.title: M&A
mk-deal-2.body:
Ostrander Media Inc. (A), a US film and television group, recently announced its intention to acquire the video-game developer Hartsell Games Inc. (B). The news came suddenly and there was no anticipation effect. The deal is expected to be completed or to fail in exactly 1 year from now. If the deal goes through, every 5 shares of B will be exchanged for 2 shares of A. If the deal fails, prices will return to their original levels.

Share prices before the announcement were PA,0 = $72.00 and PB,0 = $25.00. Immediately after the announcement the market incorporated the new information: PA,1 = $68.50 and PB,1 = $26.50. The one-year risk-free rate is rf = 4%.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is A's offer worth per B share at the prices immediately after the announcement? What premium over B's price before the announcement is that, in percent?
parts.solution:
Every 5 B shares become 2 A shares, so one B share becomes 2/5 = 0.4 A shares.

Offer value = 0.4 × $68.50 = $27.40 per B share. Premium = 27.40/25.00 − 1 = 9.60%.

B trades at $26.50, below the offer, because the deal may fail. Since A pays in shares, A's fall from 72.00 to 68.50 has cut the offer from 0.4 × 72.00 = $28.80 (a 15.20% premium) to $27.40.
criteria: Exchange ratio per B share 2/5 = 0.4 A shares (5/2 = 2.5 is the ratio turned upside down).
Offer value 0.4 × 68.50 = $27.40 at the prices after the announcement and a premium of 9.60% over $25.00 (1 point each).
Using A's old price (28.80 and 15.20%) gives the offer at the old prices, not at the prices after the announcement.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Based on the market prices, calculate the probability of the deal being successfully completed as perceived by the market. (Hint: use a long-short strategy and invest the proceeds from the short sale at the risk-free rate.)
parts.solution:
Step 1. Build the position at the prices after the announcement. The exchange ratio tells you how to pair the legs: 5 B shares against 2 A shares.

LegActionCash flow today ($)
Long targetBuy 5 B shares at 26.50−132.50
Short acquirerShort-sell 2 A shares at 68.50+137.00
Risk-freeInvest the 137.00 at 4%−137.00
Net outlay−132.50

Step 2. The deal goes through. The 5 B shares are converted into 2 A shares, which close the short. Only the deposit is left: 137.00 × 1.04 = 142.48.

Step 3. The deal fails. Prices return to 72.00 and 25.00. You buy back 2 A shares for 144.00 and sell 5 B shares for 125.00: 142.48 − 144.00 + 125.00 = 123.48.

Step 4. The certainty equivalent. The strategy cost 132.50 today, so its expected payoff in one year must equal 132.50 × 1.04 = 137.80. Do not plug in 132.50.

Step 5. Solve. 137.80 = p × 142.48 + (1 − p) × 123.48
p = (137.80 − 123.48)/(142.48 − 123.48) = 14.32/19.00 = 0.7537 (75.37%)

Check. 0.753684 × 142.48 + 0.246316 × 123.48 = 137.80 ✓. B at 26.50 lies between its failure price 25.00 and the offer value 27.40.

The traps. Plugging in 132.50 instead of 137.80 gives 0.4747. Ignoring the interest altogether (no deposit growth and no certainty equivalent) gives 0.7632.
criteria: Long 5 B and short 2 A, because the exchange ratio is 5 for 2; the short-sale proceeds of 137.00 are invested at the risk-free rate. Other consistent constructions are accepted (for example 1 B against 0.4 A).
Success payoff 137.00 × 1.04 = 142.48: the converted B shares close the short.
Failure payoff 142.48 − 144.00 + 125.00 = 123.48, at the prices before the announcement.
Certainty equivalent 132.50 × 1.04 = 137.80. Plugging in 132.50 gives 0.4747, the error Kurbatov's key calls out.
p = 14.32/19.00 = 0.7537. Reasonable approximations are fine.
This part is worth 10 of the 20 points, so show the whole construction: the position, both payoffs, the certainty equivalent and the equation.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Based on the market's reaction to the announcement, what could be the reason for this deal? (There can be several answers: choose one reason (not synergies!) and explain it briefly in 2–3 sentences.)
parts.solution:
Read the reaction first. A fell from 72.00 to 68.50 (−4.86%) and B rose from 25.00 to 26.50 (+6.00%). The market sees the deal as bad for A's shareholders and good for B's: value moves from A to B.

Model answer (empire building). Ostrander's CEO may want to turn a film and television group into a larger entertainment group and buy a game developer for size and prestige rather than for value, so A pays more for B than B is worth to A. B's shareholders collect the premium and B may gain access to A's distribution and marketing, which is why B rises while A falls. This is an agency problem between A's managers and A's shareholders.

Also accepted. Any reason other than synergies that fits A down and B up, as Kurbatov's H2025 key puts it: «Plenty of possible reasons». For example managerial hubris or overconfidence and the winner's curse; diversification that A's shareholders could get more cheaply by buying game shares themselves; paying with A shares the managers think are overvalued, which the market reads as bad news about A; coinsurance, where the merger makes A's debt safer at the expense of A's shareholders; B's managers being weak, so that B gains from any new owner. Not accepted: synergies, «value creation» without a mechanism, or tax losses, which are erased on a change of owner.
criteria: Uses the reaction as evidence: A down and B up, so the market sees the deal as inefficient for A and B's shareholders extract the benefits.

One reason other than synergies, explained in 2–3 sentences, that fits A down and B up. Any such reason is accepted (the H2025 key: «Plenty of possible reasons»): empire building, hubris or overconfidence, the winner's curse, unnecessary diversification, paying with overvalued A shares, coinsurance, or B gaining access to a larger firm's resources.
Not accepted: synergies, «value creation» alone or tax losses.
Keep it to 2–3 sentences; length is not rewarded.

parts.label: d
parts.body: You are a shareholder of A. A's largest shareholders force a vote on whether A should proceed with the deal. Based on the reason you chose in (c), how would you vote? How will the market react to the result if most other shareholders vote like you? Briefly explain.
parts.solution:
Minimal accepted answer. With the reason in (c) the deal moves value from A's shareholders to B's, so as a shareholder of A I vote against. If most others vote the same way, the deal is blocked and prices return towards their levels before the announcement: A up towards $72.00 and B down towards $25.00.

For full marks. The reversion may be incomplete. An entrenched management may try to go ahead anyway, so a small chance of completion survives. The bid may also have revealed that B is worth more than the market thought, or attract another bidder, so B can stay above $25.00.

Consistency. The vote must follow from the reason in (c). If you argued there that A's fall was a temporary overreaction, a vote in favour with the matching market reaction is also defensible.
criteria: Votes against and gives the reason: the deal is inefficient for A's shareholders, who you are.
Answers the second question too: prices revert towards their original levels (A up towards 72.00, B down towards 25.00). This is the minimal accepted answer.
The vote must be consistent with the reason in (c).
Bonus: an entrenched manager may proceed anyway, so prices do not fully revert; the bid may have revealed that B was undervalued, so B stays above its old price.

mk-deal-3.title: M&A
mk-deal-3.merke: Mannesmann-formen med variantene Kurbatov nevnte i forelesning 16 (1:14:18) og i wrap-up (5:29)
mk-deal-3.body:
Carrowmore Insurance plc (A) has made a surprise offer for Ellisford Assurance plc (T): if the deal goes through, every 2 T shares will be exchanged for 5 A shares. The deal will be completed or fail in exactly six months; if it fails, both prices return to their pre-announcement levels.

Before the announcement PA,0 = £13.80 and PT,0 = £30.00; just after it PA,1 = £14.60 and PT,1 = £35.10. The risk-free rate is 4.5% a year, compounded annually. Short selling is allowed and fractions of shares are fine. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the offer worth per T share at today's prices? What is the spread to T's price, in £ and in percent of T's price?
parts.solution:
One T share becomes 5/2 = 2.5 A shares.

Offer value = 2.5 × £14.60 = £36.50 per T share.
Spread = 36.50 − 35.10 = £1.40, or 1.40/35.10 = 3.99% of T's price.

The spread is what a buyer of T earns over six months if the deal goes through, before interest. It is the market's compensation for the risk that the deal fails.
criteria: Exchange ratio 5/2 = 2.5 A shares per T share; 2/5 is the ratio turned upside down.
Offer value 2.5 × 14.60 = £36.50 at today's A price.
Spread £1.40 and 3.99% of T's price, as the question asks (in percent of the offer it would be 3.84%).

parts.label: b
parts.body: You trade without money of your own: for each T share you buy, short-sell the A shares it converts into, pay for T with the proceeds and invest the rest at the risk-free rate. How much do you invest? What is the position worth in six months if the deal goes through? If it fails?
parts.solution:
Step 1. The position today.

LegActionCash flow today (£)
Short acquirerShort-sell 2.5 A shares at 14.60+36.50
Long targetBuy 1 T share at 35.10−35.10
Risk-freeInvest what is left−1.40
Net cash flow0

You invest £1.40 per T share, which is the spread from (a). Nothing comes out of your own pocket.

Step 2. Six months of interest. T = 0.5: 1.0450.5 = 1.022252. The deposit grows to 1.40 × 1.022252 = 1.4312.

Step 3. The deal goes through. The T share becomes 2.5 A shares, which close the short. Only the deposit is left: £1.4312.

Step 4. The deal fails. You sell the T share at 30.00 and buy back 2.5 A shares at 13.80, which costs 34.50: 1.4312 + 30.00 − 34.50 = −3.0688, a loss of £3.0688. You owe more on the short than the T share and the deposit are worth.

Check. The two payoffs differ by 34.50 − 30.00 = 4.50, the loss on the shares if the deal fails. A position that costs nothing must be able to lose money, or it would be an arbitrage.
criteria: Short 2.5 A for each T, T paid with the proceeds: 36.50 − 35.10 = £1.40 invested at the risk-free rate and a net cash flow of 0 today.
Success: 1.40 × 1.022252 = £1.4312, since the converted T share closes the short.
Failure: 1.4312 + 30.00 − 2.5 × 13.80 = −3.0688 (£), a loss, at the prices before the announcement.
2 points for each number; the construction must be shown.

parts.label: c
parts.body: What probability of completion do today's prices imply? (If you could not solve (b), use £1.50 for success and −£3.00 for failure.)
parts.solution:
Step 1. What the price must satisfy. The position costs nothing today. If the market prices it fairly, its expected payoff in six months must therefore be zero: the certainty equivalent of a cost of 0 is 0.

Step 2. Solve. 0 = p × 1.4312 + (1 − p) × (−3.0688)
p = 3.0688/(1.4312 + 3.0688) = 3.0688/4.5000 = 0.6820 (68.20%)

Check. 0.681966 × 1.431153 − 0.318034 × 3.068847 = 0.0000 ✓.

With the values given in the question. p = 3.00/(1.50 + 3.00) = 0.6667 (66.67%), full marks if the method is right.

The traps. No interest at all gives 0.6889. A full year of interest (1.045) gives 0.6749: wrong, but it is the error already penalised in (b). Simple interest, 1 + 0.045 × 0.5, gives 0.6819, close enough.
criteria: The position costs 0 today, so its expected payoff must be 0 (no certainty equivalent to compute).
Follow-through: with the values given in the question, p = 0.6667. A student who used 1.045 for six months in (b) gets 0.6749 here and loses the points for the factor only once, in (b).
Reasonable rounding is fine; show the equation.

parts.label: d
parts.body: A colleague instead pays for one T share with her own money, short-sells the same A shares and invests all the proceeds at the risk-free rate. What probability does her position imply? Compare with (c) in one sentence.
parts.solution:
Her payoffs. She deposits 36.50, which grows to 36.50 × 1.022252 = 37.3122 (success). If the deal fails: 37.3122 + 30.00 − 34.50 = 32.8122.

Her certainty equivalent. She paid 35.10: 35.10 × 1.022252 = 35.8811.

p = (35.8811 − 32.8122)/(37.3122 − 32.8122) = 3.0688/4.5000 = 0.6820

Comparison. The same probability as in (c). Her position is yours plus a risk-free deposit of £35.10, which pays 35.8811 whether or not the deal goes through, so it adds nothing about the deal. Both ways are equally correct, as the lecture says about this variant (recording 16, 1:21:33).
criteria: Her payoffs 37.3122 and 32.8122, certainty equivalent 35.8811 and p = 0.6820 (2 points).
Explanation (1 point): her position is yours plus a risk-free deposit of 35.10 that pays the same in both states, so the implied probability cannot change.
Leaving out the certainty equivalent (plugging in 35.10) gives 0.5084, which is wrong. Using 1.045 again gives 0.6749: the same factor error as in (b), penalised only there.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Just after you trade, the regulator says it needs one more year: the deal will be decided 18 months from today. How would you treat this? If prices did not move, would the implied probability be higher or lower than in (c)? Why? Why would prices probably move anyway? (3–4 sentences, no calculation needed.)
parts.solution:
Model answer. The position and the payoffs on failure stay the same, but the deposit now grows for 1.5 years instead of 0.5, so I use 1.0451.5 = 1.068254 in place of 1.0450.5. With unchanged prices the implied probability is lower: the spread earns interest for longer, so the same spread can pay for a larger expected loss, while the loss on failure (4.50) is fixed. The prices would probably move anyway, because a delay is news: more can go wrong over 18 months (the regulator may block the deal, a rival may bid, A's shareholders or financing may turn), so the market is likely to lower p and T's price would fall relative to the offer.

The numbers, not required. Unchanged prices: success 1.40 × 1.068254 = 1.4956, failure 1.4956 − 4.50 = −3.0044, so p = 3.0044/4.5000 = 0.6677, down from 0.6820. With p unchanged the spread would instead narrow slightly, to (1 − 0.6820) × 4.50/1.068254 = 1.3397: in a share offer both legs are discounted, so time value alone does not widen the spread. It widens if the market lowers p.

Bonus. The assumption that prices return to their levels before the announcement is weaker after 18 months, since both firms keep operating and news arrives.

The lecturer raised this tail in the wrap-up (recording 18, 5:29): «What if we can delay this M&A by one year? How would you treat it?», with an intuition-based answer in mind.
criteria: Treatment (1 point): same position and failure prices, but the money grows for 1.5 years: 1.045^1.5 = 1.068254 instead of 1.045^0.5.
Direction (1 point): with unchanged prices p is lower (about 0.6677). Saying that p rises because there is more time to complete the deal is wrong.
Reason (1 point): the spread earns interest for longer, so it covers a larger expected loss, while the loss on failure is fixed.

Why prices move (1 point): the delay is news and more can go wrong, so the market is likely to lower p and T's price falls relative to the offer. Bonus: the reversion to the old prices is less credible after 18 months.

mk-governance-1.title: Governance
mk-governance-1.merke: Samme form som eierspørsmålet i forelesning 17 (1:18:44): «select three things and elaborate»
mk-governance-1.body: You founded and own all of Vantrell Health Software, which makes booking systems for hospitals. Next year Vantrell will list on a US exchange: you will keep 35% of the shares and the rest will be widely held. You will hand the CEO job to an outsider and stay on the board.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Select three things you would put in the new CEO's contract or in the way the company monitors the CEO. Elaborate each in about three sentences: how it makes the CEO act in the shareholders' interest and its main drawback (2 points each). Leave share classes out; they come in (b).
parts.solution:
Three things, each with how it works and its drawback. As a 35% owner you capture 35% of any gain from monitoring, so free riding is not your problem.

1. An independent board. Most of the 7 to 11 directors have no ties to the CEO, the chair is not the CEO and independent committees handle audit, pay and nominations. Such directors can question the CEO, set the pay and fire the CEO without being the CEO's friends; the lecture calls this «one of the first check marks» (recording 17, 1:19:39). Drawback: outsiders know less than the CEO and depend on the CEO's own information, so they can miss problems or block good projects.

2. Long-term equity pay with a clawback. Much of the pay comes as restricted shares that vest over four to five years, with bonuses that can be taken back if results are restated. The CEO's wealth then rises and falls with the long-run share value, like yours. Drawback: the share price also moves with the market and luck, so the CEO bears risk outside the CEO's control and must be paid more for it.

3. Your own monitoring, written into the bylaws. Proxy access lets large shareholders put director candidates on the company's ballot; an annual investor meeting lets you and the institutions question the CEO. The CEO knows that the owners can replace directors, while the institutions get a reason to vote. Drawback: monitoring that is too tight makes the CEO passive, doing only the safest things (recording 17, 1:17:10).

Other things that score. Options, with their own drawback (they reward excessive risk); a bonus on targets with clauses against gaming (EPS raised by a share buyback does not count); a golden parachute if Vantrell needs the CEO to take R&D risk; transparency and regular reporting; limits on perks such as private use of a company jet; the CEO on the board but never as chair. «Make the shareholders vote» earns the points only with a how: investor meetings, communication, proxy access or the institutions, since small owners cannot be forced (recording 17, 1:20:22 to 1:21:51).
criteria: Three distinct things, about three sentences each, 2 points each: 1 for how it makes the CEO act in the shareholders' interest and 1 for a real drawback. A thing without a drawback earns at most 1 of 2.

As in Kurbatov's H2025 key for the same kind of question: «Any reasonable action with explanation should be accepted». Examples (recording 17): an independent board and its committees, the CEO not as chair, restricted shares, options, clawbacks, bonuses with clauses against EPS gaming, a golden parachute for R&D risk, transparency and reporting, limits on perks, proxy access in the bylaws, special meetings, investor meetings with the owners.

Counting: two versions of the same tool with the same drawback count once. Restricted shares and options count as two things if the drawbacks given differ (for example market luck against excessive risk-taking). Share classes earn nothing here, since (b) asks for them.
«Make the shareholders vote» counts only with a concrete how; without one it earns at most 1 of 2.
Board size: an argument with both sides is accepted (about 7 to 11 directors). «A smaller board works better» alone is not accepted.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Your bank suggests two share classes: you keep B shares with ten votes each and the new investors buy A shares with one vote each. Give one argument for and one against this structure, seen from the new outside shareholders (2–3 sentences each, 2 points each).
parts.solution:
For. The structure lets you sell 65% of the cash flows and still control the firm (about 84% of the votes), so the long-term plan is protected against short-term pressure and hostile bids. The lecture gives the Ford family as the example: it raised a lot of capital and kept control with a small share of the equity. The lecture calls dual-class shares «not a completely stupid measure» (recording 17, 1:19:49).

Against. Votes are separated from cash-flow rights: you carry 35% of the cost of a bad decision but hold about 84% of the votes. The outside shareholders cannot replace the board, win a proxy fight or sell to a hostile bidder, so a poor CEO you back or your private benefits cannot be stopped: the firm is entrenched.

Also accepted. For: investors buy knowing the terms, so the price they pay already reflects them; the structure protects the people and culture a software firm depends on. Against: the A shares are likely to trade at a discount; the control lasts after the founder's skill or interest fades, unless the B shares convert to one vote after some years (a sunset).
criteria: For (2 points): control and the long-term plan are protected from short-term pressure and hostile bids while the firm raises capital. Noting that investors buy knowing the terms is optional.

Against (2 points): votes are separated from cash-flow rights, so the founder bears only part of the cost of bad decisions and the outside owners cannot use their vote, proxy fights or the takeover market: entrenchment.
Seen from the outside shareholders, as the question asks. «It is good for the founder» alone earns at most 1 of 2.
Bonus: a sunset clause, or noting that the votes are about 84% for 35% of the equity.

mk-governance-2.title: Governance
mk-governance-2.merke: Samme form som kontraktsspørsmålet i forelesning 17 (35:23): hvordan lønnen styrer CEO-en
mk-governance-2.body:
Aldwyn Aero Engines Inc., a US-listed maker of aircraft engines with dispersed ownership, is developing an engine that will burn 20% less fuel. The programme will take eight years and may fail. The board proposes this pay package for a new CEO:

  1. an annual cash bonus of up to 100% of salary if earnings per share (EPS) grow by at least 8% in the year;
  2. an annual bonus of up to 50% of salary tied to the company's score from an independent ESG rating agency;
  3. a golden parachute: three years' pay if the CEO is fired.

For each element, explain in 2–3 sentences what it encourages the CEO to do and how it can backfire or be abused (3 points each). Then say in one sentence which element you would change first as a long-term shareholder and how (1 point).
mk-governance-2.solution:
1. EPS bonus. It pushes the CEO to raise earnings every year, which is simple to measure and tied to profits. But it invites short-termism: the CEO can lift EPS mechanically with a share buyback that cuts the number of shares, even an inefficient one, or cut spending on the eight-year engine programme to raise this year's earnings. The lecture warns that a CEO will «do everything in their power to achieve this bonus and nothing else» (recording 18, 1:13:49).

2. ESG bonus. It rewards real changes the rating agency can see and here points the same way as the business, since an engine that burns less fuel is both greener and cheaper for airlines to run. It backfires because ratings are noisy and can be raised by reporting and box-ticking. Pay for a score that is not tied to value can also make the CEO spend shareholders' money on what the agency checks.

3. Golden parachute. It protects the CEO if a risky but valuable programme fails, so the CEO does not avoid the R&D risk the engine needs; the lecture recommends it for exactly this kind of firm (recording 17, 16:18). It backfires because it rewards failure: the CEO is paid even after poor effort or reckless bets. Three years' pay also makes it costly for the board to fire the CEO or for a bidder to take over, which protects a weak CEO.

Change first. The EPS bonus, since it is the easiest to abuse and works against an eight-year programme: measure performance over several years, exclude the effect of buybacks and pay the bonus in restricted shares. Any other choice with a reason is accepted.

Also accepted. For 1: managing accruals or delaying maintenance. For 2: an ESG score is much harder to game than EPS, since raising a governance score means actually improving governance (recording 17, 38:23); a score built for other stakeholders can conflict with shareholder value, so whose interest is the CEO serving? For 3: a parachute only on a takeover, or one capped or tied to the programme's milestones, limits the abuse.
criteria: 3 points per element: 1 for what it encourages and 2 for how it backfires or is abused, with the mechanism. A label alone («short-termism», «moral hazard») earns at most 1 of the 2.
EPS: a share buyback raises EPS mechanically by cutting the number of shares; cutting R&D or maintenance lifts this year's earnings at the cost of the engine programme.
ESG: rewards real change and here fits the fuel goal; it backfires through noisy ratings, box-ticking or spending at the shareholders' expense. Saying it is harder to game than EPS is optional.
Golden parachute: encourages the risk the programme needs; backfires by rewarding failure or low effort and by making it costly to fire the CEO or to take the firm over.

The last point: one element to change first, with how. The EPS bonus with a multi-year target, no credit for buybacks or pay in restricted shares is the natural answer, but any reasoned choice earns the point.

mk-governance-3.title: Governance
mk-governance-3.merke: Teoriformen fra H2024 E2 og H2025 E2 (setningsbudsjett og poeng per del), med stoffet fra forelesning 17, 1:08:04
mk-governance-3.body:
Two US-listed firms adopt the same poison pill: if anyone buys over 15% without board approval, all other shareholders get one new share per share.

  • Orrin Fusion is in year six of a nine-year plan to build a fusion plant. Its losses are as planned and reported quarterly; most owners are long-term pension funds. After a hedge fund pushing for quick payouts began buying, 78% of votes approved the board's pill.
  • Mallory Home Goods has lagged its peers for five years. Its CEO chairs a board with five executives among nine directors. The board adopted the pill overnight without a vote, two days after a private equity firm disclosed a 9% stake.

parts.label: a
parts.body: How does the pill stop a hostile bidder? (2–3 sentences)
parts.solution: Once a bidder crosses 15%, every other shareholder gets one new share per share, so the number of shares nearly doubles while the bidder's stake does not: 15% becomes 15/(100 + 85) = 8.1%. Much of the money it paid for its shares is lost to the other owners. Buying control on the market becomes far too expensive, so the bidder has to negotiate with the board, which can withdraw the pill; in effect the board gets a veto over any takeover.
criteria: Mechanism (1 point): crossing 15% triggers new shares for everyone except the bidder, which dilutes the bidder's stake (to about 8%) and its value.
Consequence (1 point): a takeover without the board's consent becomes too costly, so the bidder must negotiate with the board, which can remove the pill.
Kurbatov's words fit: the pill forces the bidder «to the table of negotiations» (recording 17, 30:13).

parts.label: b
parts.body: For each firm, is the pill more likely to protect shareholder value or to entrench the managers? (2–3 sentences and 3 points per firm)
parts.solution:
Orrin: more likely to protect the shareholders' value. The losses are planned and reported, so they do not signal poor management; a bidder could buy in year six before the plant earns anything and cut the programme or the research team just before it pays off. The owners themselves approved the pill, the firm is transparent and the owners are stable and long-term, which is when the lecture says entrenchment can be positive: it preserves the vision and the human capital (recording 17, 1:08:35 to 1:10:54). The cost is weaker outside monitoring, so the board and the owners must watch the CEO more closely.

Mallory: more likely to entrench the managers. Five years of lagging peers suggests poor management, which is exactly what a takeover would discipline by putting in a better team. The board is captive (the CEO chairs it and a majority are insiders) and it adopted the pill overnight without asking the owners, two days after a bidder appeared, so the pill mainly protects the managers' jobs and private benefits. The other shareholders lose the takeover premium and the threat that keeps the managers in line.
criteria: 3 points per firm: 1 for the right verdict and 2 for the reasons drawn from the case.

Orrin: protects value; planned and reported losses, a vote by the owners, stable long-term owners and a long programme that a bidder could cut (positive entrenchment). Naming the cost, weaker external monitoring, is a bonus.

Mallory: entrenches; long underperformance means the takeover threat is the discipline needed, the board is captive (CEO as chair, insiders) and the pill came overnight without a vote right after the stake was disclosed.
An answer that calls both pills bad, or both good, earns at most 3 of 6: the question tests that the same defence can serve different interests.

parts.label: c
parts.body: How should each share price react to the pill? (1–2 sentences)
parts.solution: Mallory's price should fall: the market reads the pill as entrenchment and lowers the chance of a takeover premium; the lecture notes that the market reaction to such pills is usually very negative (recording 17, 22:51). Orrin's price should react little, or even rise, since the owners approved the pill and it protects the programme; a small fall for the lost takeover premium is also accepted with that reason.
criteria: Mallory (1 point): the price falls, because the pill signals entrenchment and removes the expected takeover premium.
Orrin (1 point): a small or no reaction, or a rise, because the owners approved it and it protects the programme; a small fall is accepted if it is explained by the lost chance of a takeover premium.
The direction must be consistent with the verdicts in (b).
